title: What If the National Curriculum Did Its Job?
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that the familiar symptoms of English schooling (teachers planning from scratch, curriculum leads rebuilding the national curriculum locally, a booming market in uneven teacher resources, and assessment and inspection quietly redefining what counts) are not failures of workload or professionalism but evidence of incomplete system-level design. Using Jaques' levels of work and Richard Claydon's Run/Serve/Change language, he frames the National Curriculum as an attempt at S4 'Change work' that stops short because curriculum, assessment, inspection and accountability are governed as separate systems and because political time horizons reward ambiguity. The cost of that unfinished work is displaced downward: school leaders become curriculum architects and integrators, and teachers absorb the interpretive burden. He sets out what proper S4 curriculum work would look like (specified depth and limits, shared exemplars and non-exemplars, integrated assessment design) and insists this is not a call for central micromanagement but for usable boundaries that relocate judgement to where it belongs. He then turns to what school leaders can do now, which is to settle curriculum judgements locally so planning becomes adaptation rather than invention, and closes by reading the 2025 Curriculum and Assessment Review as echoing the diagnosis while stopping short of its structural conclusion.
points: Hart reframes teacher-created resource websites as structural problem-solving rather than entrepreneurialism: teachers are compensating for missing shared curriculum boundaries, not outsourcing thinking for lack of expertise.
The ambiguity of the National Curriculum is presented as a political necessity at S6 level that looks like professional trust but is paid for downstream as planning effort and defensive teaching.

Hart distinguishes genuine Change work (decisions that settle recurring problems once) from improvement activity like new schemes of work or training, which repeats precisely because it never removes the underlying ambiguity.
Strong boundaries are argued to make professional freedom usable rather than reduce it, relocating judgement toward pedagogy, adaptation and response to learners.
The practical leadership task is to stop absorbing unfinished national work into people by deciding locally which knowledge, sequence and depth will be settled and centrally resourced.
quotes: This post explores my claim that England’s National Curriculum is an attempt at system level Change work but one that stops short. The result is that complexity is pushed down into schools, where it is absorbed as planning effort, interpretation and improvisation.

At the highest level, national curriculum design operates under short political time horizons, contested legitimacy and intense public scrutiny. Precision is risky; ambiguity and a call for interpretation is safer.
What can be sold as autonomy is ambiguity forced downwards. And ambiguity, when combined with accountability, carries a significant cost.
The explosion of teacher created resources is often framed as creativity or entrepreneurialism. It is better understood as problem solving.
A National Curriculum doing its job fully would not micromanage classrooms; this is undesirable on lots of levels. It would do something harder.

Proper S4 curriculum work does not replace professional judgement; it relocates it. It settles a small number of integrative decisions once so that teachers and leaders are free to exercise judgement where it actually belongs: in pedagogy, adaptation, response to learners and local context.

When Change work is incomplete at the top, someone still has to do it. The only question is whether it lives in systems and curated documentation or in people; that is the real cost of ambiguity and it is why Change work matters.
